articles.title: Free Family Food-Growing Workshops Coming to Newton-le-Willows and St Helens
articles.body:
Families in Newton-le-Willows and St Helens can get hands-on with food growing during Green Libraries Week. The Coalfields Regeneration Trust's free workshops explore how changing weather patterns affect fruit and vegetable growing, with seed sowing, take-home activities and children's puzzles.

Newton-le-Willows Library hosts a session on Saturday 24 October, 11am–noon; Chester Lane Library in St Helens follows on Monday 26 October, 2–3pm. Places must be booked in advance with the relevant library, by email or at the counter.

KS Garden Services tip: Even a small sunny patch or a few containers can be a good starting point for growing food at home.

Image credit: Illustrative seed-sowing photograph by USDA (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons. File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Sowing_seeds_into_container_trays_(3821447364).jpg · Licence: Public domain

articles.title: Common Ivy Tops UK Pollinator Survey: Why Autumn Flowers Matter
articles.body:
An eight-year UK Pollinator Monitoring Scheme analysis has found that common ivy received the most insect visits among 14 widespread flower types recorded in ten-minute surveys. Hogweed, bramble, buddleja, knapweeds and thistles were also popular. The findings, highlighted by wildlife charity Buglife on 15 October, show why late-season flowers are valuable when other nectar sources are scarce.

Gardeners need not leave every climber unchecked: manage ivy where it threatens structures or smothers young plants, while keeping safe flowering patches where practical. Buddleja can support butterflies but should be deadheaded after flowering to limit self-seeding.

KS Garden Services tip: Before autumn cutting, look for ivy in flower and consider leaving some blooms for visiting insects.

Image credit: Common ivy in flower with a visiting honeybee, MurielBendel, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hedera_helix_flower_honey_bee.jpg · Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

articles.title: Frances Tophill Leads Gardeners’ World with Autumn Garlic and Perennial Vegetables
articles.body:
The 16 October edition of BBC Two's Gardeners' World put Frances Tophill in the lead, with practical autumn jobs including growing garlic in containers and establishing perennial vegetables. The episode also explored plants that maintain colour and interest later in the year, as well as propagation and shade-loving planting.

For smaller gardens, container garlic offers a way to try home-grown produce without dedicating a full vegetable bed. Perennial edibles can return for multiple seasons when matched to the site and maintained properly.

KS Garden Services tip: October is a good time to plan next year's productive planting areas, improve drainage and choose suitable containers before winter.

Additional reading: https://www.theguardian.com/tv-and-radio/2026/oct/16/tv-tonight-quentin-tarantino-makes-a-rare-appearance-on-graham-nortons-sofa

Image credit: Illustrative potted garlic photograph by Ericamack1986, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (not a BBC programme image). File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Garlic_in_pot.jpg · Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

articles.title: Autumn Container Makeovers: Simple Planting Ideas for Colour Through Winter
articles.body:
A fresh 16 October gardening feature highlights autumn as a good moment to rethink tired pots. Rather than replacing everything, a longer-lasting display can combine a structural evergreen or ornamental grass with hardy perennials, trailing foliage and spring bulbs. Large containers give roots more space and can be easier to manage through seasonal changes.

The RHS recommends winter-friendly options such as violas, pansies, compact daffodils, heucheras and hardy ferns. Use peat-free compost suited to the plants, ensure drainage holes are clear and raise pots on feet so they do not stand in winter water.

KS Garden Services tip: A well-planted entrance pot can brighten a garden without committing to a complete border redesign.

Additional reading: https://www.rhs.org.uk/container-gardening/winter-selection

Image credit: Illustrative viola in a planter photograph by Tael, CC0 (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons. File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Flower_in_a_planter.JPG · Licence: https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/

articles.title: New Chinese Scholars’ Garden Opens at RHS Bridgewater Near Manchester
articles.body:
RHS Garden Bridgewater in Salford opened its Yangzhou Scholars’ Garden to visitors on 26 September 2026. More than eight years in the making, it is the centrepiece of the Chinese Streamside Garden and brings traditional Yangzhou garden design, craftsmanship and planting to Greater Manchester.

The surrounding landscape features more than 200 trees and shrubs and nearly 4,000 perennials, selected for seasonal interest and cultural meaning. For North West gardeners, it offers a nearby opportunity to see how paths, water, structure and planting can work together in a thoughtfully designed space.

KS Garden Services tip: Even a modest garden can borrow the design principle of framing a view with a path, feature plant or seating area.

Image credit: Illustrative Chinese garden pavilion at Hamilton Gardens, New Zealand (NOT RHS Bridgewater), photograph by Pseudopanax, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons. File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pavilion_in_Chinese_Scholars'_Garden.jpg · Licence: Public domain

articles.title: UK Breeding Bird Indicator Down 19% Since 1970: Five Ways Gardens Can Help
articles.body:
New figures published by Defra on 13 October show that the UK's breeding bird indicator has fallen by 19% since 1970. Farmland and woodland birds have experienced major long-term declines, with renewed pressure on several groups in recent years. The figures measure changes in a basket of species, rather than a count of every bird in the country.

Local gardeners can make small but useful changes: keep some seedheads and berry-bearing shrubs through winter, grow varied plants, retain safe shelter, and keep bird water clean. Avoid removing all the cover from borders during autumn tidy-ups. A wildlife-friendly garden can still look cared for.

KS Garden Services tip: Clear paths and lawns where needed, but leave selected stems and sheltered corners for wildlife.

Image credit: European robin photograph: Deepak Sundar, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (illustrative). File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:European_Robin_looks.jpg · Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

articles.title: RHS Research: Which Garden Trees Offer the Best Climate Benefits?
articles.body:
New research released on 12 October by the RHS and tree nursery Frank P Matthews tested 19 popular garden trees for benefits such as cooling, shelter, rain interception and wildlife support. Every tree provided a measurable benefit in at least one area. Callery pear 'Chanticleer', flowering cherry 'Fugenzō' and red maple 'Brandywine' performed strongly for cooling; Italian cypress 'Garda' stood out for rainfall interception and screening.

The cooling measurements were taken with irrigated trees, so performance may differ in dry soil. Choose a tree for its mature size, roots, soil requirements and the space available, not simply for one research result.

KS Garden Services tip: Autumn is a good time to plan tree planting, but wait until soil conditions are suitable and make room for the eventual canopy.

Image credit: Ornamental cherry photograph: David J. Stang, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (illustrative, not a tested cultivar). File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Prunus_subhirtella_Autumnalis_8zz.jpg · Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

articles.title: St Helens Great Potato Festival — Saturday 17 October
articles.body:
Chester Lane Library in St Helens is hosting the Great Potato Festival on Saturday 17 October, from 11am to 3.30pm. The free community event brings together local growers, performers and families for a celebration of the humble spud, with potato printing, crafts, games and activities.

It is a timely reminder that growing vegetables can be sociable, affordable and enjoyable for all ages. Anyone interested in starting a small vegetable patch next year can begin planning a sunny spot with good soil and drainage now.

KS Garden Services tip: When lifting the last of your potatoes, remove damaged tubers and store sound ones in cool, dark, frost-free conditions. Check the official event page for ticket and attendance details before travelling.

Image credit: Potato harvest photograph: Fhynek00, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (illustrative, not a festival photograph). File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Potato_Harvest.jpg · Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

articles.title: New Hedgehog Study Finds Major Rural Declines — But Gardens Can Help
articles.body:
A new study published in Ecology and Evolution in October brings together five national hedgehog recording schemes. One long-running rural survey estimates a 70.7% fall in hedgehog abundance between 1981 and 2023, while another found an 80.4% decline in rural occurrence between 2002 and 2023. Some predominantly urban surveys showed modest increases, highlighting the importance of gardens and connected green spaces.

Gardeners can help by leaving a quiet log or leaf pile, keeping gaps under fences for hedgehog movement where safe, and checking thoroughly before strimming or clearing dense vegetation. Never disturb an occupied nest.

KS Garden Services tip: Before a major autumn clearance, inspect long grass, compost heaps and leaf piles carefully for wildlife.

Image credit: European hedgehog photograph: Thecalmgardnr, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons. File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:European_hedgehog_in_grass.png · Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

articles.title: Robot Mowers Get Smarter: STIGA Announces New Vista Features
articles.body:
Garden machinery manufacturer STIGA has announced two software updates for its Vista robotic mower range, scheduled before the end of 2026. Planned features include improved camera-based obstacle avoidance, mowing schedules for individual garden zones, new cutting patterns and encrypted live video through the STIGA.GO app. The upgrades are intended for existing Vista machines as well as new ones.

The announcement shows how robotic mowing is becoming more adaptable, but automated machines still need appropriate setup, safe operation and routine checks. Traditional mowing, edging and seasonal lawn care remain important for many gardens.

KS Garden Services tip: When comparing robot mowers, check connectivity charges, obstacle detection, servicing and suitability for uneven lawns rather than relying on headline features alone.

Image credit: Robotic lawn mower photograph: Preetihe, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons (illustrative; not a STIGA model). File: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:HOOKII_robotic_lawn_mower.jpg · Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

articles.title: This Friday in St Helens: Learn to Save Seeds and Share Them Locally
articles.body:
A community seed-saving and botanical art workshop is taking place at Chester Lane Library, Four Acre Lane, St Helens, on Friday 16 October 2026, from 11am to 12.30pm. Green Town St.Helens is organising the session, with Emma from Emma’s Wild Garden leading the activities.

Visitors can learn how to collect and store seeds, decorate their own seed packets and contribute seeds to the Chester Lane Seed Library, helping other local gardeners grow flowers and food in future seasons. Beginners are welcome. The organiser asks for a £5 booking deposit, refunded when you attend; spaces are limited, so check availability before travelling.

KS Garden Services tip: Only save seeds from healthy, mature plants. Allow seedheads to dry, label envelopes with the plant name and collection date, and store them somewhere cool and dry. Not every hybrid variety will grow true to its parent.

Photograph: Making seed packets, Pacific Southwest Region USFWS (CC BY 2.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

articles.title: RHS Bridgewater Trial Reveals Standout Hydrangeas for Autumn Colour
articles.body:
After five years of testing at RHS Garden Bridgewater in Greater Manchester, the Royal Horticultural Society has published its 2021–2025 trial results for Hydrangea paniculata. Twelve cultivars gained the RHS Award of Garden Merit, including BONFIRE, PASTELGREEN, REDLIGHT and SKYFALL.

The trial looked at plant health, vigour, flower colour and shape, and how well different varieties performed. Panicled hydrangeas are known for large, cone-shaped flowerheads that often change from white or green towards pink as they age, bringing interest from late summer into autumn.

For local gardens, the RHS advises planting in spring or autumn in moist but well-drained ground. Light shade works well, though a sunnier position can suit plants where the soil does not become too dry. The soil does not need to be acidic. Pruning last year’s growth in early spring can encourage larger flowers, but severe pruning is not essential for every garden.

KS Garden Services tip: Choose a hydrangea for its eventual size as well as its flowers. This avoids unnecessary hard cutting every year.

Photograph: Hydrangea paniculata (illustrative, not a named trial winner), Max071086 (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

articles.title: STIHL's ALLPRO Batteries: Faster Charging for Professional Gardeners
articles.body:
Battery garden machinery continues to develop, and STIHL's ALLPRO system highlights just how quickly professional charging technology is moving. STIHL says its ALLPRO Performance batteries can reach 80% charge in as little as nine minutes when used with the AL 1802 MO high-speed charger under the specified conditions.

That headline figure applies to particular ALLPRO Performance batteries rather than every battery in the range. STIHL also states that the new ALLPRO batteries work with existing AP System tools, while charging speed depends on the battery and charger combination.

For garden maintenance businesses, quicker charging may eventually reduce the number of spare batteries needed on long jobs. However, equipment cost, weather resistance, battery weight and genuine run time still matter as much as the advertised charging speed.

KS Garden Services tip: Before buying battery equipment, check the exact tool, battery and charger combination rather than comparing headline charging times alone.

Photograph: Example of a cordless hedge trimmer (Makita model, not STIHL), Mark Hunter (CC BY 2.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

articles.title: North West Bird Watching Festival Returns to Martin Mere This Weekend
articles.body:
WWT Martin Mere near Burscough will host the North West Bird Watching Festival on Saturday 17 and Sunday 18 October 2026. The event celebrates autumn migration, when pink-footed geese and other wetland birds gather across the reserve.

The programme includes talks, guided walks, wildlife photography and opportunities to see species such as pintail, shoveler and pochard. WWT says visitors may see thousands of pink-footed geese moving between their roosting and feeding grounds. Check the official programme and ticket details before travelling.

Although a garden is very different from a wetland reserve, both benefit wildlife. In local gardens, seedheads, berry-producing shrubs and safe sources of water can help visiting birds through the colder months. Keep water clean and avoid disturbing sheltered habitats unnecessarily.

KS Garden Services tip: An autumn tidy-up does not have to mean stripping every border bare. Leave selected stems and seedheads where they will be attractive, safe and useful to wildlife.

Photograph: Pink-footed geese in flight in Lancashire, Apricaria (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

articles.title: David Domoney's October Plant Picks: Flowers, Berries and Autumn Foliage
articles.body:
TV gardener David Domoney has shared his October 2026 selection of plants that can keep gardens colourful as the season changes. His recommendations include Heuchera villosa 'Autumn Bride', Mahonia 'Jungle Whisper', Pyracantha 'Saphyr Jaune' and Acer griseum.

These plants show that autumn interest is about more than late flowers. Heuchera 'Autumn Bride' carries airy white flower sprays over attractive foliage, mahonia can provide architectural leaves and flowers, pyracantha offers colourful berries, and paperbark maple (Acer griseum) is prized for peeling cinnamon-brown bark and autumn leaf colour.

Plant choices should match the garden's soil, light and space. Some larger shrubs and trees are not suitable for a very small border, while thorny plants need careful positioning beside paths and play areas.

KS Garden Services tip: For a garden that looks good for longer, combine flowering perennials with plants chosen for foliage, bark and wildlife-friendly berries.

Photograph: Heuchera villosa 'Autumn Bride', Krzysztof Ziarnek, Kenraiz (CC BY-SA 4.0), via Wikimedia Commons.

articles.title: Still flowering in October? Meet the Cornish lily!
articles.body:
Just look at that splash of pink! While many summer flowers are starting to fade, the Cornish lily (Nerine bowdenii), also called Bowden lily, comes into its own during autumn.

Its distinctive, curled petals can brighten borders in September and October — proof that the garden still has plenty to offer long after summer ends.

How to grow Cornish lilies:
• Position: choose a sunny, sheltered spot.
• Soil: free-draining soil helps bulbs thrive, particularly over winter.
• Planting: avoid burying bulbs too deeply — leave the neck exposed in a suitable sheltered position.
• After flowering: remove spent flowerheads and let the leaves die back naturally.
• Best tip: leave established clumps undisturbed for a good display in future years.
